questions.question: A coastline is measured with dividers: a drawing tool with two legs set a fixed distance apart, walked along the coast step by step. The distance between the legs is halved again and again. What happens to the measured length?

options.text: It settles on one fixed value, as the length of a circle does
options.why: Settling is what a smooth curve such as a circle does. A coast does not settle: its measured length keeps growing.

options.text: It shrinks, because each shorter step leaves out more of the coast
options.why: A shorter step leaves out less of the coast, not more. It fits into small bays that a longer step went straight across.

options.text: It keeps growing, as shorter steps follow bays longer ones cut across
options.why: On one map of Britain the measured length went from 17.7 to 33.4 as the step was halved four times. A smaller step finds smaller bays, and the total never settles.

options.text: It stays the same, since the coast itself does not change at all
options.why: The coast does not change, but what a step of a given size can follow does. The number of steps grows faster than the step shrinks.

questions.question: Points of the plane can be treated as numbers, called complex numbers, which can be squared and added. The Mandelbrot set is made of the points c for which the rule 'start at zero, square, add c, repeat' stays within 2 of zero. The Julia set of c comes from the same rule with c fixed and the starting point changed: it is made of the starting points that stay. What does the Mandelbrot set say about the Julia sets?

options.text: Which values of c give a Julia set in one piece, and which give dust
options.why: For c inside the Mandelbrot set, the Julia set of c holds together in one piece. For c outside, it breaks into separate specks, like dust. The walk from zero stays within 2 exactly when the Julia set is in one piece.

options.text: Which starting points escape for one single fixed value of c
options.why: That describes one single Julia set. The Mandelbrot set changes c and always starts the walk at zero.

options.text: How many steps each Julia set takes to be drawn on a screen
options.why: The colour bands outside the Mandelbrot set count the steps needed to escape, for each c. Whether c is in the set depends on whether its Julia set holds together.

options.text: Which Julia sets fill a whole area, with a dimension of exactly 2
options.why: The Mandelbrot set does not sort the Julia sets by dimension. It sorts them into those in one piece and those that are dust.

questions.question: A Lichtenberg figure is the branching mark an electric discharge burns into glass or wood. A computer grows one point by point: at each step one point next to the figure joins it. The chance for a point is proportional to the strength of the electric field there, raised to a power η (eta), called the field power. The field is strongest at the tips. What happens when η is raised above 0?

options.text: Every point next to the figure becomes equally likely to join it
options.why: Equal chances belong to η = 0, since any number raised to the power 0 is 1. Raising η moves away from that, towards the tips.

options.text: The figure branches more often, grows bushier and its dimension rises
options.why: It goes the other way. A bushy figure comes from a low η, a thin needle from a high one.

options.text: Growth stops being random, so every run gives the very same figure
options.why: Each new point is still picked by chance, so no two runs match. The power η changes the chances, not the randomness.

options.text: The tips win more new points, the figure thins and its dimension falls
options.why: A higher power favours the strongest field, which is at the tips, so the figure thins towards a single channel. Its dimension, a number that measures how much of the area the branches fill, falls from 1.603 at η = 0.6 to 1.208 at η = 2.0.

questions.question: The Sierpinski carpet starts from a square cut into a 3 by 3 grid of 9 smaller squares. The middle one is removed and the other 8 are kept, and the same cut is repeated in every kept square, without end. For a shape made of N copies of itself, each 1/k as wide, the dimension d is the power that k must be raised to in order to give N. What is the dimension of the carpet? (log stands for the logarithm, which finds such a power.)

options.text: 8/3, about 2.667, the number of copies divided by 3
options.why: The dimension is a power, found with logarithms, not a ratio. A value above 2 would mean more than a filled square.

options.text: log 8 / log 3, about 1.893
options.why: Here N = 8 and k = 3, so 3 to the power d must be 8. That gives d = log 8 / log 3 = 1.893.

options.text: log 3 / log 8, about 0.528
options.why: This turns the formula upside down. The number of copies goes on top, because 3 to the power d must equal 8.

options.text: log 3 / log 2, about 1.585
options.why: That is the Sierpinski triangle: 3 copies, each half as wide. The carpet keeps more of itself, so its dimension is closer to 2.

questions.question: A square is cut into a 3 by 3 grid. The centre square and the four squares in the middle of each side are kept, 5 in all, and the four corners are removed. The same cut is repeated inside every kept square, without end. For a shape made of N copies of itself, each 1/k as wide, the dimension d is the power that k must be raised to in order to give N. What is d? (log stands for the logarithm, which finds such a power.)

options.why: The dimension is a power, found with a logarithm. The plain ratio of the two numbers is not it.

options.text: log 5 / log 2, about 2.322
options.why: This uses copies half as wide. Here each copy is one third as wide, so the base is 3.

options.text: 2, because the pieces are squares
options.why: The shape of the pieces does not decide it. Keeping 5 of 9 squares at every step leaves far less than a filled square.

options.text: log 5 / log 3, about 1.465
options.why: The rule gives 5 copies, each one third as wide. So 3 to the power d is 5, and d = log 5 / log 3 = 1.465.

questions.question: The Koch curve starts from a straight segment of length 1. At every step each piece is replaced by 4 pieces, each one third as long: the middle third of the piece is lifted into a point with two sides. How long is the curve after 3 steps?

options.why: Each step multiplies the length by 4 × 1/3 = 4/3. Three steps give (4/3)³ = 2.37. A fixed factor above 1, repeated, has no upper limit.

options.text: 2, adding one third at each step
options.why: The length is multiplied at each step, not increased by a fixed amount. Each step adds a third of the current length, and that length keeps growing.

options.text: 64, the number of pieces
options.why: 64 is the number of pieces, but each is only 1/27 long. The length is the number of pieces times the length of one.

options.text: 1, because the curve stays inside the same rectangle
options.why: The rectangle never changes, but the curve crinkles inside it. A curve kept inside a small region can still grow longer without limit.

questions.question: Box counting lays a grid of square boxes over a shape and counts the boxes the shape touches. At one box size a shape touches 200 boxes. With boxes half as wide it touches 566. Halving the boxes multiplies the count by 2 to the power d, where d is the dimension. What is d? (log stands for the logarithm, which finds a power.)

options.text: About 2.83, the factor the count grew by
options.why: 2.83 is the factor itself. The dimension is the power that turns 2 into 2.83.

options.text: About 0.67, log 2 / log 2.83
options.why: This turns the formula upside down. The growth of the count goes on top, and the factor 2 below.

options.text: About 1.50, log(566/200) / log 2
options.why: The count grew 566 / 200 = 2.83 times, and 2 to the power 1.5 is 2.83.

options.text: Exactly 2, since the boxes are squares
options.why: A filled area would touch 4 times as many boxes when they are halved. 2.83 is less than 4, so the shape lies between a curve and a filled area.

questions.question: The Mandelbrot set is tested by a walk: start at 0, then again and again square the number and add c. If a value ever gets further than 2 from zero, the walk escapes and c is outside the set. A point c outside is coloured by the number of steps until that happens. For c = 0.5 the walk gives 0.5, 0.75, 1.06, 1.63, 3.15. What is its count?

options.text: 4, since 1.63 is close enough to 2
options.why: 1.63 is still less than 2. The test has one threshold, and only a value above 2 counts.

options.text: 5, since 3.15 is the first value above 2
options.why: 3.15 is the first value past 2, so 0.5 is outside the set and its count is 5. Points nearer the edge of the set take more steps to escape.

options.text: No count: 0.5 is in the set, since it is less than 2
options.why: c being less than 2 does not decide it. The walk from zero must stay within 2 for ever, and this one leaves.

options.text: 1, because the first step already lands on c
options.why: Every walk from zero lands on c at the first step. The count is the first step whose value is further than 2 from zero.

questions.question: The Barnsley fern is drawn by four moves. Each move shrinks, turns and shifts a point. One point is moved again and again, by a move picked at random each time, and every place it lands is marked. The same fern appears whatever the starting point, even one far away. Why?

options.text: Each of the four moves brings any two points closer, so the start is forgotten
options.why: Each move shrinks distances by a factor below 1: 0.160, 0.851, 0.341 and 0.379. Distances shrink at every step, so from any start the points are pulled onto the same shape.

options.text: The moves are picked at random, and over many steps the chance evens out the start
options.why: The same list of random moves, run from three different starts, gives the same fern. The shrinking does the work. The random choice only decides where on the fern the next mark lands.

options.text: The second move is picked 85 times in 100, so it alone decides the shape
options.why: That weighting explains why most marks come from the second move. It does not explain why the start is forgotten, and all four moves shape the fern.

options.text: The starting point is first moved onto the fern, before any drawing begins
options.why: There is no such step. A start well away from the fern, even a whole circle or square, ends on the same fern.

questions.question: Box counting lays a grid of boxes over a shape and counts the boxes it touches. On the edge of the Mandelbrot set it gives a dimension of 0.919, 1.055 and 1.114 on pictures 256, 512 and 1024 pixels wide. The dimension, a number that measures roughness, is proved to be exactly 2. What explains the gap?

options.text: Box counting does not work on curves at all, so the three numbers mean nothing
options.why: Box counting gave 1.228 on the coast of Britain, next to 1.232 from walking dividers along it. It works on curves. Here it has not yet reached its final value.

options.text: The true dimension is about 1.1, and the proof of 2 is only an estimate
options.why: A proof is exact. Numbers that climb as the picture gets finer are short of the answer, not at it.

options.text: The edge has detail at every scale, so no finite picture reaches the limit
options.why: Each finer picture finds more detail, and the measured value climbs with every step up in resolution. Magnified 1074 times, the edge still shows new spirals, so any grid misses some. The value is known by proof, not by counting.

options.text: The edge is smooth, a smooth curve has dimension 1, so 2 is an error
options.why: Only the outline of the main body of the set is smooth. The whole edge carries thin threads at every scale, and its dimension is 2.
